However, in the previous section on the seventh [cause], the "predominant condition" (*adhipati-pratyaya*), at its conclusion—

Commentary: Next, the name "aids to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*) is explained.
For the sake of sentient beings, one diligently seeks liberation,
taking nirvāṇa as the cause;
nirvāṇa is termed liberation.
As is commonly discussed,
because one diligently seeks that which is consistent with this and does not contravene that practice, it is called "conformity" (*ānulomika*).
"Part" (*bhāga*) refers to the cause.
It is a "part" (*aṅga*).
Regarding the term "part of the aids to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
"part" refers to that which is a part of penetration (*nirvedha*).
This refers to the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). "Factor" (*aṅga*) has the meaning of a constituent part;
it is so called because it accords with that stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
They are called the "Aids to Penetration" (nirvedhabhāgīya).
Here, the term "aid" (*bhāga*) has the sense of a causal factor;
they are the causes for liberation.
Because it is one branch of the cause,
it is called a "factor" (aṅga); that is,
being conducive to the essence [of the path], it is a factor.
That which accords with the portion of liberation is called the "stage conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
This is based on altruism as its cause.
One seeks liberation in order to deliver sentient beings;
however, seeking bodhi makes the benefit of others manifest,
while diligently proceeding toward liberation increases the benefit for oneself.
However, regarding the discussion of self-benefit in relation to bodhi and the implication of benefiting others through nirvāṇa,
it is intended to show by means of the latter that bodhi likewise benefits sentient beings.
By this, it is shown that Nirvana is also capable of benefiting oneself;
for the phrasing here reflects the meaning as it extends to that [Nirvana]. Question: Why is the "factor conducive to liberation" (mokṣabhāgīya) called "conducive"?
Question: Is the essence of the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) not itself an aid? Answer: The essence of penetration is conditioned (saṃskṛta).
Since penetration can be the essence of the "aids," and because its essence possesses multiple parts, it is called an "aid."
The essence of nirvāṇa is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
liberation is not a constituent part of it, because its essence is neither one nor many. Furthermore, that which is called "liberation" is the mental factor of resolute confidence (*adhimokṣa*).
Liberation through the condition of liberation from suffering is called "liberation" (*vimukti*).
When it is designated by its object within the causal state, it is called "resolute confidence" (*adhimokṣa*).
Because it serves as the cause for emerging from suffering in the resultant state, it is called "liberation."
If one follows this interpretation, liberation itself is designated as the "limb of liberation" (mokṣabhāgīya).
However, the meaning of "limb" (bhāga) here is not the same as that of the "limbs conducive to penetration" (nirvedhabhāgīya);
rather, it is named in relation to wisdom (prajñā).
If this is designated by the name "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*), then the aforementioned difficulty does not arise.
Although the preceding section has set forth the essential nature and boundaries of the stages (*bhūmi*) and explained the two different names for these stages, [the following continues:]

Regarding this stage of the bodhisattva reaching the cultivation of bodhisattva practices,

This explains the four powers.

these are precisely the innate and acquired lineages previously mentioned.
He has already encountered and served immeasurable Buddhas appearing in the world;
this is the power of the spiritual friend.

That which cannot be shaken or destroyed by evil associates is called the power of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
It is said that because such a person has already well accumulated all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*),
the Bodhisattva who has well cultivated the provisions of merit and wisdom (*puṇya-jñāna-saṃbhāra*) [is so described].

It refers to the roots of virtue and so forth that have been well-accumulated by means of the three causes previously explained in the immediately preceding section.
Vasubandhu says:
The first power acts as the cause;
the second power acts as the condition;
and the third power enables the cultivation of correct practice.
The fourth power is that by which, through the accumulation of roots of goodness, one is called a bodhisattva who has gathered the provisions;
thus it is said to be by the power of mental attention (*manasikāra*) that one thoroughly cultivates the two kinds of provisions: merit and wisdom.
The ability to enter the ten stages is due to the power of the foundational support;
these four, in comparison to the nature of the two vehicles,
constitute the conditions of evil friends.
The spontaneously occurring mind and the lower stage of the provisions;
because all are superior, they are called the four superior powers.
In this stage, although one has deep faith and understanding regarding the meaning of consciousness-only based on these four powers,
one has not yet realized that both forms of grasping are empty.
When one dwells extensively upon various coarse activities with a mind distracted by signs and phenomena, this is called practicing the bodhisattva path by abiding in the external gate.
As the verse in the "Ninth Decade on the Ten Abodes" (*Daśabhūmika-sūtra*) of the *Avataṃsaka* states:
The fourth is the truly noble son of the Buddha,
born from the true Dharma of the worthy and holy ones;
he has no attachment to the existence or non-existence of phenomena.
"Abandoning birth and death, they emerge from the triple world.
In the tenth chapter of that sutra, it further explains the bodhisattva at the initial stage of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*),
and the same applies to the remaining stages.
The verse says:
The pure and wondrous Dharma-body manifests in various forms.
Just like a great master of illusion,
there is nothing he does not manifest according to his will;
in some places, he brings sentient beings to the ultimate fulfillment of the bodhisattva path.
Or again, he manifests his initial birth,
his renunciation, and his practice of the path;

In some instances, he manifests entry into *nirvāṇa* for the sake of sentient beings.

How is it that this text says he dwells extensively in the external gate while cultivating the bodhisattva practices? Answer: This refers to the fourth stage (*vihāra*), wherein the bodhisattva performs ten kinds of contemplative methods.
The seventh is the contemplation of karma;
the eighth is the contemplation of its fruits,
which subdues the active entanglements of the present.
Not relying on ignorance regarding the path of seeing and so forth,
one no longer creates evil karma that would cause future results to arise;
this is called abandoning birth and death and emerging from the three realms.
It is certain that one will be able to emerge from what is not the proper time, having already emerged;
even now, practicing the bodhisattva path by way of the external gate does not contradict this.

Furthermore, these bodhisattvas of the ten stages also possess a small portion of reliance upon contaminated meditative concentrations (*sāsrava-samādhi*) that enables them to manifest the eight aspects [of a Buddha] to deliver sentient beings; this is because,
within the first stage of the ten stages, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*),...
Having attained the ten powers, they train in ten dharmas.
The tenth dharma is to act as a place of refuge for suffering sentient beings.
Having established themselves in this, those bodhisattvas [proceed].
Progressing through successive stages of increasing excellence, they are able to practice the eight aspects;
however, they mostly engage in distracted conduct and rarely succeed in entering meditative concentration to perform the contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*).
It is said that they "mostly dwell in the external gate," but this does not mean that those bodhisattvas dwell exclusively in the external gate; thus,
there is no contradiction.

Commentary states:
Due to this matter, the active manifestation of the two types of grasping serves as the perfuming that induces the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Yet, there is as yet no power capable of subduing and extinguishing these two underlying tendencies so as to prevent the active manifestation of those two types of grasping from arising. Question: In the tenth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within the section explaining the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the Bodhisattva...
It is said that all afflictions are eliminated and forever exhausted without remainder;
it is the unimpeded contemplation of tranquil extinction.
This is the Buddha’s true Dharma.

How is it that this statement has not yet subdued the two types of grasping? Answer: It is said to exhaustively describe the category of afflictions associated with the uncommon ignorance that arises based on the causes of false teachings and false teachers, even though [that ignorance] has been subdued.
It is not that all afflictions arising from one's own conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) are exhausted;
furthermore, it is taught that the power of the Buddha-dharma can extinguish all afflictions.
It is not that one is already able to extinguish all afflictions at the stage of the ten abodes;
rather, according to this treatise, although the two types of conceptual grasping are gradually suppressed and extinguished during the path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*).
Because they have not yet been fully subdued,
the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states: "Regarding those ordinary persons within the internal dharma who are heedful,
I do not say that their volitional formations are conditioned by ignorance."
Regarding the statement that "the non-common, associated ignorance of self-discrimination, the views, and so forth,
can be suppressed at this stage," the present explanation says they are not suppressed because they arise due to false teachings.
Furthermore, regarding the complete classification of innate [afflictions] and so forth as objects of abandonment, it is stated only in general terms;
for the most part, they cannot yet be said to be "unsubdued," nor can it be said that even a small portion is unsubdued.
The subsequent section of the treatise states:
"It is only at the stage of application (*prayoga*) that one is first able to suppress the dualistic grasping of conceptualization;
for those who follow false teachings, such grasping arises even during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*)."
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that a bodhisattva practicing through resolute belief may still give rise to afflictions due to lapses in three areas,
and at times may even abandon their precepts.
The various dharmas described are like shooting in the dark, where one may or may not hit the mark;
therefore, within this stage, the afflictions of one's own conceptualization are not yet exhausted.
This correctly explains the latter two lines of the verse.
Treatise:
These two terms, "grasping" (*grāha*), extend to the nature of the grasped (*grāhya*).
Commentary: [As stated above.]

If one speaks only of "the two graspings" when referring to the "two graspings," there are seeds of the two graspings that are not grasping;

Furthermore, since the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and so forth are not necessarily subject to subdual,

What is the meaning of "latent tendency" (anuśaya)?
It refers to that which follows sentient beings, constantly remaining within the cycle of birth and death;
it lies dormant and hidden within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), not manifesting elsewhere.
Therefore, they are called *anuśaya*.
Alternatively, they are called *anuśaya* because they increase faults;
they follow along with sentient beings and greatly increase their transgressions.
Therefore, they are called "latent tendencies" (anuśaya).
Why is it that "to lie dormant" (śayana) carries the meaning of "increase"?
It is like a person who is fond of sleep; as they sleep, their slumber increases.
Therefore, the increase of faults is the meaning of *anuśaya*.
In the former case, the name is established by indicating its essential nature;
in the latter, it is derived from a metaphor as its cause.
The differences from the Sarvāstivāda are as recorded in separate excerpts;
these are precisely the seeds of the two hindrances.

Commentary states:

With the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as the foremost and the view of a self as the root, all afflictions arise.
If the view of a self is absent, the afflictions are accordingly severed; they are abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
The principle is the same here:

although the delusions produced by [the view of self] may have been previously eliminated, the view of self itself has not yet been extinguished; it is only upon reaching the stage of ultimate exhaustion that the view of self is severed, whereupon the remaining delusions are finally and completely eradicated.
Although these [afflictions] are abandoned separately according to their nine grades,
when one abandons eight grades and so forth, it is taught that the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is not abandoned;

Because the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has no distinct grades and is severed only upon the complete abandonment of desire; furthermore, since the delusions produced have many grades,
the views that produce them must likewise certainly possess nine grades.
This is because, as one gradually abandons the nine grades of self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) in accordance with the abandonment of desire,
when the root is severed, the others are also severed accordingly. In this context,
it is not called "self-view" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), but rather "view of a personal identity" (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
If one says that the view of self does not include the notion of "mine," the Sanskrit term is *mamedṛṣṭi*,
which is translated here as "the view of self."
In Sanskrit it is called *satkāya*;
here it is translated as "the view of a self that shifts and moves unrealities," which includes the notion of "mine."
In order to reveal that this [view] includes what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), it is called *satkāya*. Regarding the one hundred and twenty-eight root afflictions:
there are forty to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the desire realm.
There are thirty-six types in each of the higher realms, plus sixteen for the path of cultivation,
totaling one hundred and twenty-eight kinds,
along with their outflows and various secondary afflictions (upakleśa).
These consist of twenty types,
or even more,
as explained in the previously cited *Śrāvakabhūmi* (Section on the Compendium of Bases).
This arises from its own intrinsic nature;
as for its retinue and other minds and mental factors, they have the five aggregates as their nature.
This is stated in the seventh chapter of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*.

that treatise broadly designates both the primary factors and their remote attendants as "obstructions" (āvaraṇa) by way of conventional designation.

It ought to be the nature of defilement;

Since that is not the case, this current text is superior.

Commentary states:

Regarding "view, doubt, ignorance, craving, hatred, pride, and so forth":
this indicates their essential nature (*svabhāva*).

yet in reality, since the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) cannot be separated from ignorance (*avidyā*), it must necessarily have a specific number.
Moreover, this serves to clarify that the grasping at phenomena is itself ignorance.
Among the five ground-abidings (*pañca-vāsanā-bhūmi*), it is subsumed under only one abiding.

If that is so, why does it not mention the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)? Since "pride and so forth" is stated, it implies the inclusion of the secondary afflictions by way of the term "and so forth."

This arises from the essence of self-nature.

"All minds and mental factors,
as well as the karma produced thereby..."
All resulting fruits are subsumed within this,
for all are rooted in the ignorance of clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha-avidyā*).
In this context, "fruits" refers to the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*),

What is called the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)?
The treatise states:
that which conceals the objects of knowledge is termed the cognitive obscuration.
The commentary states:

Second is the explanation of the names. Regarding the "objects of knowledge," these refer to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which possess the nature of non-perversion.
It refers to the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
Because it obscures this object such that wisdom does not arise, and because it is able to obstruct bodhi, it is called the "obstruction to the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

"Because this cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) reaches such a state of being subtle and weak."
The commentary states:
Third, the analysis of the causes of the eight consciousnesses refutes external attachments.
The eighth consciousness is named the *vipāka-vijñāna* (retributive consciousness).
Why do they not arise simultaneously?
Because that ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is subtle, feeble, and weak,
whereas this grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is coarse and strong in comparison to it.
Because this [consciousness] is capable of being perfumed (*vāsana*), that [other consciousness] is not.
Masters such as Sthiramati maintain that the minds of all three natures (*trisvabhāva*) possess attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*);
however, this [eighth] consciousness is exclusively the result of maturation (*vipāka*).
The treatise refutes it solely within the category of maturation (vipāka),
because [maturation] is not associated with ignorance (avidyā) or wisdom (prajñā).
The commentary states:
All treatises maintain that this eighth consciousness is associated with only five mental factors,
and that its cognitive nature is necessarily one of attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha).
Furthermore, it is conjoined with ignorance;
while wisdom is capable of conceptual deliberation,
ignorance causes delusion.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"There is an interpretation that the grasping at dharmas (*dharma-grāha*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) pervade all three natures."

This is because both the categories of contaminated mind and the categories of uncontaminated mind belonging to the two vehicles fail to fully comprehend the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
All [these] arise from the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) as if they were the object-part (nimitta-bhāga),

these do not exist within this obstruction.
However, to refute and suppress that position, the Master of Dharma merely states:
"If one says that attachment to dharmas [occurs], what need is there for it to be accompanied by wisdom? Thus says the treatise.

Since it is admitted that this [consciousness] arises simultaneously with the eighth consciousness,
the seventh possesses attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
When the wisdom realizing the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*) arises, it no longer functions.
The eighth [affliction] is the grasping at phenomena as real;
when the wisdom realizing the emptiness of phenomena arises, this [grasping] should be extinguished.
Since the eighth manifests simultaneously with that [wisdom], [it cannot be eliminated].
It is known with certainty that the eighth consciousness is not accompanied by the grasping of non-existence (*anupalambha-grāha*).
The formal proof (*pramāṇa*) states:
"The eighth consciousness, etc."
It is certainly not a category of clinging to dharmas, because it arises simultaneously with the contemplation of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmāśūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

It is like the Buddha’s eighth consciousness; if one were to say that when the contemplation of the emptiness of dharmas arises within the causal state, the eighth consciousness is permitted to be severed.

Nor can it be said that the perfuming occurs together with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*),
for that consciousness is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because it has not yet been attained.

so it should be with the ripening of the other consciousnesses.

it cannot serve as an analogy.
Regarding this treatise, it is superior even to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
As for the treatise,
it states that among the seven transformative consciousnesses, they are explained as being like the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The commentary states:
Since there is no grasping that arises separately from the afflictions,
their number is equal to that of those afflictions.
Among the seven consciousnesses, there are four fundamental [afflictions],
eight secondary afflictions,
and the discernment of the specific object-consciousnesses.
There are thirteen mental factors.
The sixth consciousness possesses all of them;
the five sensory consciousnesses possess three primary factors and ten secondary afflictions.
It is associated with thirteen factors.
Why, then, do the five consciousnesses lack seeing, doubt, and so forth?
[The] Treatise [says]:
The five consciousnesses, beginning with the visual consciousness, are all capable of inducing [conceptualization].
The commentary states:
because they lack deliberative conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).
The view of phenomena (*dharmadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and so forth are definitely not associated [with these consciousnesses].
The phrase "and so forth" includes the various afflictions (*kleśa*) that arise intermittently (*paryavasthāna*).

That is to say, the ten [mental factors] such as anger in their entirety, and a portion of the other ten,
which are produced by investigative discrimination (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*),
are entirely absent from the five sensory consciousnesses.

It is not that the various afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing are called "non-conceptual" because within the path of seeing there is no objectifying of false friends or teachers as being one's own conceptualized afflictions.

Thus, there is the delusion of discrimination;
however, it does not arise through its own power,
because it is produced by being led by the mental faculty (manas).
Therefore, the *Śāstra* states: "The others are all capable of being induced by the power of the mind.
The term "others" refers to those other than [the afflictions of] view and doubt.
This is explained in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
Although the five consciousnesses lack seeing and so forth,
they are induced by the mental consciousness and thus possess non-seeing [factors] such as craving and aversion, which are subsumed under the two hindrances;
this is what is meant here.
In addition to those [afflictions], there are other afflictions arising from one's own power and conceptualization;
this is to refute the externalist view that holds the afflictions within the five sensory consciousnesses are severed only through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Thus says the treatise.

"By means of the four thorough investigations and the knowledge of reality as it is..."
Regarding the mental verbalization of the meaning that resembles [external] words and objects,
one is then able to realize that there is only the nature of consciousness (*vijñaptimātratā*).
That same fascicle further states:
The four investigations (paryeṣaṇā) occur during the stages of Heat (uṣmagata) and Summits (mūrdhan);
true knowledge (bhūtajñāna) occurs during the stages of Patience (kṣānti) and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma).
This treatise is likewise the same.
Thus, even the knowledge of reality as it is (yathābhūta-jñāna) is included among the outflows (sāsrava).
This is stated in the tenth dwelling (*vihāra*) of the forty-eighth fascicle:
"Abiding in this dwelling, one attains the extremely pure patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
What, then, is this? It refers to how bodhisattvas, having correctly investigated all phenomena through the four investigations, [proceed as follows].
Having previously attained the four types of knowledge in accordance with reality,
one understands all phenomena as they truly are;
at that time, all false conceptualizations and attachments are completely abandoned.
"In the present life, one accords with the contemplation of the non-arising of all afflictions," and so forth,
as explained at length.
This knowledge of reality begins from the stage of conduct through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
Up until this point, there has been application and effort,
and the state has not yet reached ultimate purity;
however, within this present stage, it has already attained ultimate purity, and for this reason it is called "the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thus, the knowledge of reality as it is (yathābhūtajñāna) is the essence of the realization of non-arising (anutpattikadharmakṣānti).
However, in its actual sense,
this investigation pertains only to that which is with outflows (sāsrava).
It is investigated solely by the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*),
because it is neither fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) nor subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Because they comprise the preparatory, fundamental, and subsequently attained wisdoms,
here only patience (*kṣānti*) can be the fruit,
while that [wisdom] alone is the cause as the preparatory stage.

In the seventy-third [fascicle], it is stated that only the untainted (*anāsrava*) is taken as the essence of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), without mentioning that it also extends to the tainted (*sāsrava*).

Elsewhere, according to the actual state of affairs, it extends to both the tainted and the untainted. The stage prior to receiving confirmation is called the arising of investigative patience (*vitarka-kṣānti*); at the time of receiving confirmation, it is called suchness-wisdom (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
Although middle patience also contemplates the absence of a grasper,
it has not yet reached definitive confirmation;
nevertheless, because there was prior confirmation, it is also termed "actual wisdom."
It is not that vitarka is associated with vitarka;
otherwise, the stages above would lack the levels of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*.
This is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśat-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-bhāṣya*.
Because of a deficiency in application and because they do not manifest before them, the foolish person [is unable to realize] these four types of knowledge of reality as it is.
There are then eight kinds of false discrimination,
which can produce three things and give rise to the world of sentient beings as well as the receptacle world.
If one understands this, the eight types of conceptualization and so forth are eliminated.
These points are explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
The treatise says:
Regarding the four thorough investigations (*catasraḥ paryeṣaṇāḥ*), it is said that they reach the point where [things] exist only nominally and lack substantial reality.
The commentary states:
this refers to the names and meanings of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).
Since, in the preceding stage, one takes the objects of the dharma and its meaning as the focal point,
that which appears therein as the text— the meaning of the names of the text— is solely mental discourse;
and that which relies upon the meaning of these names of the text is likewise solely mental discourse.
The *Ṣaṣṭhavyākhyāna* by Asvabhāva states:
"In this context, 'name' refers to the investigation of names, as well as the causes and effects of names, such as form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth.
The 'causes of names' refer to syllables (*akṣara*), word-bodies (*padakāya*), multi-word-bodies (*vākyakāya*), sounds (*śabda*), and so on."

The eleventh [chapter] of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "That which is called 'fruit' refers to phrases (*pada*), as well as name-bodies (*nāmakāya*), multiple name-bodies, phrase-bodies (*padakāya*), and multiple phrase-bodies."

This means that when one investigates the individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the collections of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*) of all phenomena (*dharma*), none are found to be substantially real.
A name merely designates a phenomenon;
it simply refers to the investigation of names.
"Meaning" (artha) refers to that which is expressed by the name-groups (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
Whether it be their substance (*svabhāva*) or their meaning, these are collectively termed "meaning.
Because "meaning" is broad in scope, its own substance is not mentioned [separately].
Upon investigation, one finds that this signifier and its signified are certainly not interconnected.
Here, one contemplates only the signifier and signified as they are grasped by deluded attachment; these are of the nature of mere mental verbalization.
Since it is not said that the dependent nature of words and meanings within mental verbalization does not exist,
one should now observe that, based upon the signifier and the signified,
these are in fact of the nature of mental verbalization alone.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises state that this occurs during the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*). In these stages,
because one contemplates only the non-existence of the apprehended object (*grāhya*), one contemplates the non-existence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
It does not depend on another;
for otherwise, it would constitute a perverted mind,
as it would be viewing that which exists dependently as non-existent.
Wu-xing says:
"One investigates that the external objects signified by names are of the nature of mental discourse (*manojalpa*) alone;
for while one contemplates this meaning as it manifests with the semblance of external forms, in reality it exists only within."
It is not that there is no internal textual meaning dependent on others.
These two exist only as internal phenomena;
because they are designated by provisional names as external phenomena possessing textual meaning, they are said to be merely provisional.
This means that all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are subsumed within these objects.
This encompasses all existing phenomena.
By means of these two types of phenomena, one observes their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), finding that there is nothing external to the mind.

These are merely provisional designations, just like the self (*ātman*); the same applies to the distinctions in the essence of phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth, such as the meaning of impermanence (*anitya*).
As Wu-xing said:
One realizes that the four kinds of false appearances are subsumed within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
and one thoroughly understands that the four kinds of imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) are all unattainable.
As stated in the "Chapter on the Thirty-Six True Meanings":
These bodhisattvas contemplate those names and objects either by way of their distinct characteristics or by way of their combined characteristics.
Because one accomplishes the contemplation of the aspect of synthesis, one penetrates the two kinds of intrinsic natures and the two kinds of conventional designations for their distinctions.
This is because, through the contemplation of the aspect of separation, one contemplates the two kinds of intrinsic natures individually.
Since one has already previously engaged in the four investigations through preparatory application,
and since there must necessarily be the fruit of wisdom following these four investigations,
the fruit of wisdom is now explained next.
Treatise:
To thoroughly know things as they truly are is called "knowing them as they truly are.
Commentary: [This means that]...
In the preceding four investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*), one contemplates that the four objects of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) do not exist apart from consciousness;
thus, one contemplates only the absence of the grasped (*grāhya*) without yet contemplating the grasper (*grāhaka*).
This wisdom of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) confirms that the aforementioned objects do not exist apart from consciousness.

Once the grasped object is realized as empty, one is further able to thoroughly know that the grasping subject—that consciousness—is devoid of an internal objective realm; thus, the grasping subject is also empty.
One then realizes that the internal consciousness and its transformed manifestations are inseparable from one another.
The characteristics of consciousness-only, such as illusory phenomena and the like, are known to be like illusions;
once this is understood, one realizes that upon this dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) there is no imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is termed the "twofold emptiness.
Taking this as the gateway, one contemplates the principle of emptiness therein and enters the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This exists within the four roots of goodness;
it merely resembles the contemplation of the three natures,
for true reality has not yet been realized.
When there is no longer anything to be grasped during the four preceding investigations (*vitarka*),
the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) represents its subduing and elimination at the lower level,
while the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) represents its subduing and elimination at the higher level.
Because the initial stage involves subduing and eliminating the difficulty of the apprehended object (*grāhya*), it is divided into lower and upper levels;
upon reaching the stage of knowledge as-it-is (*yathābhūtajñāna*),
the lower level of patience (*kṣānti*) confirms the non-existence of the apprehended object.
In the stage of medium patience, one conforms to the contemplation of the non-existence of the grasper and subdues and eliminates the grasper.
In the stage of superior patience, one gives rise to the seal of the non-existence of the grasper.
Both are contemplations of the lower grade of knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
When one has long practiced and subdued the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*), this constitutes merely the middle stage of patience (*madhyamā kṣānti*);

at the stage of superior patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*), one then confirms [the emptiness of the object]. The Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) confirm both of the preceding two types of emptiness.
This is called the contemplation of superior-level knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
This is distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior within the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrvaka-avasthā*);
once one has entered the grounds, each [level] further possesses its own inferior and superior aspects.
This accords with what is stated in the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
once one has entered the stages, one no longer engages in conceptual investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*),
but practices only the contemplation of suchness through knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
Since the two types of grasping have already been eliminated, it is no longer necessary to contemplate only the object of grasping as being conventionally existent.
Because the two types of grasping are absent, one simply cultivates the contemplation of knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
This state remains impure prior to the seventh bhūmi.
This essence is the very essence of the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
since it has already been attained in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*),
there is no need to perform the four investigations (*catasraḥ paryeṣaṇāḥ*).

The commentary states:
this refers to the two types, namely name (*nāman*) and meaning (*artha*).
First, identity of intrinsic nature;
second, identity of differentiation.
Therefore, they are collectively termed the two kinds of intrinsic nature: the nature of the name and the nature of the meaning.
And the two distinctions constitute the contemplation of synthesis.
The former two are the name and the object;
the latter two are the intrinsic nature and the distinction.
The investigation of names and the investigation of meanings are what is sought.
"Manifest seeking" means to seek.
These two involve reflection and discernment.
"Self-nature" and "differentiation" refer to the act of reflection and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*).
"Reflection" means examination, deliberation, and observation.
Because these two mental factors involve seeking, various treatises state that they are called "investigation of names and meanings" and "examination of names and meanings," and so forth.

Below this, the fourth section explains the names of the four stages (*bhūmi*).
Treatise:
Because one relies on the concentration of "attaining clarity" (*ālokalabdha-samādhi*) to reach [this stage], it is also called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
The commentary states:
"Attaining clarity" refers to the meditative concentration.
Investigation is wisdom;
therefore, it is called "arousing.
That which occurs simultaneously with this is also called "arousing."
Just as the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma) is termed "immediate concentration" (ānantarya-samādhi) and so forth,
"clarity" (vidyā) refers to untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā).
Because it is the initial attainment of the characteristic of clarity that is untainted wisdom, it is called "attainment of clarity" (vidyā-lābha).
The concentration that attains clarity is called the "concentration of attaining clarity.
Within this state, one first contemplates the four dharmas as being dependent on others.
All are transformations of one's own mind.
These are merely provisional designations for names, meanings, intrinsic natures, and distinctions;
in reality, the nature of names, meanings, and so forth, is entirely unattainable.
However, regarding the designation "nominal" within the dependent nature,
phenomena lack names and names lack referents.
Because there is no real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in the sense of distinct categories,
are not names, objects, and even their distinctions merely conventional (*prajñapti*)?
This is as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises regarding the attainment of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*).
According to this explanation, the term "arising" (*utpāda*) refers to the act of proceeding.
It is named after its metaphorical source:
just as when the sun first rises, there is a preceding phase of arising.

That is to say, it refers to the aspect of clarity (*prabhāsvaratā*). If one says that the aspect of the practice that arises prior to wisdom (*prajñā*) is also acceptable, we shall now rely on the former interpretation.
Thus says the treatise.
Because one reaches it by relying on the Samādhi of Increasing Radiance (*vṛddhābhāsa*), it is further named "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).
The commentary states:
"Summit" has the meaning of "the ultimate."
The meaning is easy to understand.
It is called "Increasing Light" (*vṛddhāloka*) because the appearance of light becomes increasingly intense.
All treatises agree on the points above.
Treatise:
Based on the concentration that accords with the seal, it also accords with the patience of bliss.
Commentary states:
The seal of the absence of a preceding apprehended object and the absence of a succeeding apprehending subject is called the seal of conformity to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This conformity admits of two types:
first, conformity to bliss (*sukha*).
The second is named Yinshun (Yin-accordance).
If these three grades are all termed "patience" (*kṣānti*),
they are given the name "Yinshun" because patience is established as the seal throughout the lower, middle, and upper stages.
The term "seal" (*mudrā*) applies to both the initial and subsequent stages,
whereas the words "delight" (*ruci*) and "conformity" (*anuloma*) apply only to the stage of medium patience (*madhyakṣānti*). Therefore,
when combined, they refer simply to the concentration of sealing and conforming (*mudrānulomika-samādhi*).
Furthermore, as for the distinction:
the lower grade of patience is called "seal-patience" (mudrā-kṣānti),
because that which is grasped by the seal does not exist.
Medium-level patience (*madhyamā kṣānti*) is called "delightful conformity" (*anulomābhirati*),
because one delights in the absence of a grasper and conforms to the cultivation of that [object].
When superior patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*) arises, it is simply called "sealing conformity" (*mudrānuloma*).
Because the seal (mudrā) is able to apprehend [the object] by conforming to it through contemplation,
the combination of these three patiences is termed the "seal-conforming concentration" (mudrā-anuloma-samādhi).
Patience (kṣānti) is wisdom (jñāna).
The combination of "seal" (*mudrā*) and "certainty" (*niyata*) is termed the "seal-and-certainty samādhi.
The initial and subsequent [phrases] are to be understood according to this principle.
It refers to that which definitively seals and maintains [the mind] regarding the absence of anything to be grasped (*anupādāna*).
This is the stage of inferior patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*).
That which is also compliant with the patient acceptance of joy (*anulomikī kṣānti*) within the absence of a grasper (*grāhaka*) is the stage of middle patience (*madhya-kṣānti*).
This is the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).
Regarding the "conformity" (*anuloma*) and "pervasion" (*vyāpti*), [the latter] applies to the middle and upper [stages];
pleasure (*sukha*) applies only to the middle.
Thus says the treatise.
Since there is no real object, [the subject] is established only in mutual dependence.
The commentary states:
Since the grasped object of the parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature) does not exist, [the grasper likewise does not exist].
How could that which is conceptually grasped as the grasper possibly exist? The treatise states:
"The stage of 'Patience' (kṣānti) is established as a whole at the time of 'Receptive Patience' (anulomikī kṣānti)."
The commentary states:
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says,
"Entering the samādhi of a portion of true reality."
This refers to the portion of the "unnameable" (*anabhilāpya*) that is grasped by the seal.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter eight, states: "A portion has already entered into conformity with samādhi.
That treatise explains it as follows:
As for those who have already entered one part [of this stage],
because they possess a resolute acceptance and understanding regarding the absence of anything to be grasped,
they now abide in the stage of "lower patience" (mṛdu-kṣānti).
Regarding "one part that conforms":
because it conforms to the realization of the basis for the absence of a grasper,
this refers to the subsequent stage of patience (*kṣānti*).
Therefore, the names in those texts, such as the *Viśeṣa-śāstra* and the *Mahāyāna-saṃgraha*,
differ from those used here;
for they do not separately distinguish between the two stages of medium and superior patience (*madhyama-kṣānti* and *adhimātra-kṣānti*).
This means that while medium patience (*madhyā kṣānti*) merely delights in practicing in accordance [with the truth], it lacks the seal of the non-apprehension of the grasper;
thus, it differs from superior patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*), which seals the non-apprehension of the grasper.
Although that treatise contains the phrase "partially in accordance," [it refers to this distinction].
Because it does not differentiate between the degrees of pleasure and conformity, and because it conforms to the seal [of reality],
the lower, middle, and upper grades of the seal of patience (*kṣānti*) are combined at the time of the patience of conformity (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
These three stages are collectively established as "patience" (*kṣānti*) among the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Therefore, the treatise states that when one accepts and accords with [the truth], these are collectively established as "patience" (kṣānti).
This patience applies to two stages, namely: the patience of acceptance (anumodana-kṣānti) and the patience of accordance (anuloma-kṣānti).
Therefore, these are combined and termed the "seal" (*mudrā*) in the discourse on the stage of "conformity-patience" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).

Entering the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The commentary states:
"Bondage by characteristics" refers to the characteristic aspect (nimittabhāga) binding the perceiving aspect (darśanabhāga), and so forth.
As previously stated in the fifth fascicle when proving the existence of the seventh consciousness,
all minds— whether tainted, virtuous, indeterminate, or non-virtuous—
possess the aspect of the object (*nimitta-bhāga*) as a result of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
These marks are able to bind the mind;
it is not meant that the binding by marks is itself grasping.
According to one interpretation, all eight consciousnesses possess grasping.
The binding of characteristics (lakṣaṇabandhana) pertains to the vision [aspect] across all eight consciousnesses.
Some maintain that this is not the case,
because the eight contaminated consciousnesses possess conceptual discrimination (vikalpa).
The characteristic of discrimination binds the seeing-part; this is called the "bondage of characteristics" (*nimittabandhana*).
It does not necessarily require grasping (*grāha*);
even a characteristic that is not grasped is termed a "binding factor."
Question: Should the aspects of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) also be able to bind? Answer: It is not so.
That subsequently attained wisdom is obtained only after the outflows (*āsrava*) have been severed;
its essence is neither rigid nor coarse.
It is not a portion of the object-image increased by the outflows (*āsrava*),
nor is it an object of conceptual construction; rather,
the subsequently attained seeing-portion takes all aspects as its objects for the sake of realization and understanding.
The outflows (āsrava) are not like this,
because they involve conceptual discrimination and because they coexist with the characteristics of the outflows.
Because they are increased by the outflows (*āsrava*),
and because they do not constitute the realization that has severed the outflows;
they take all objects as their domain, yet they do not realize or understand them all.
Alternatively, it is because of inference (*anumāna*).
In wholesome and non-obscured neutral states of mind, there is only direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference;
in defiled states of mind, it also extends to non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Therefore, the bonds of mutual conditioning are able to obstruct and hinder vision,
preventing it from being clear and pure,
and preventing realization and knowledge.
Therefore, there is a distinction.

All contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas that are able to bind the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) are termed "bondage of signs" (*nimitta-bandhana*). If this is so, does self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) bind itself by taking the seeing-part as its object? One interpretation holds that it is also bound.
Because they belong to the category of *sāsrava* (with outflows), some maintain that this is not the case;
[they argue] that it is not the same as the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) because [the latter] takes the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object.
Because that [object] is grasped as external,
and because it is common to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
whereas this self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), when taking the seeing part (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object, is not grasping something external.

Because it is characterized solely as that which is realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If that were so, then the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the eighth consciousness and other such direct perceptions would not be the substance of the "bondage of the objective aspect" (*nimittabandha*);
consequently, by this same logic, the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) would also be bound by the self-witnessing aspect (*svasaṃvitti*).
Because it involves conceptual differentiation;
because it is not luminously pure;
and because the seeing-portion of the mind with outflows increases the self-witnessing portion.
The bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) refers to the mind that contemplates the characteristics of the outflows (*sāsrava*);
it does not mean that "signs" refers to the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*).
When the Sūtra speaks of the entanglements of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), it refers to this.
This refers to the meaning of the four parts being mutually bound.

Otherwise, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) would not be bound by the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), because when the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti*) takes [the seeing-part] as its object, it is not termed the object-part. Regarding the bondage of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya-bandhana*):
This refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 58,
states that there are two types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
First, the outflow (*āsrava*);
second, the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*). As for "outflow," when an Arhat abandons the afflictions through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they are entirely distanced from this.
That is to say, for one who possesses latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), there is a state of lack of peace within the conscious body (*vijñānakāya*).
The unserviceability that constitutes the outflow-tainted *dauṣṭhulya* refers to the state of non-peacefulness—
the fundamental nature originally acquired— which arises from the outflows and is perfumed by the outflows at the time when the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are abandoned.
The dependence on suffering and the corresponding lack of functional capacity both become attenuated.
In the first fascicle of the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, there is the "Chapter on Latent Tendencies" (*vāsanā*) consisting of twenty-four types.
The verse of that sutra states:
"The habitual tendencies of an arhat are [abandoned] because they possess faults."
Only the Buddha alone is able to deliver [beings] and serve as the refuge for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is said in [text number] fifty-eight:
This defiled heaviness (*dausthulya*) is called the habit-energy of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*).
It is that which the followers of the two vehicles are unable to sever, and which only the Tathāgata can ultimately sever;
therefore, it is called the "habit-energy eternally severed."
This is an uncommon Buddha-dharma.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states:
"All contaminated seeds existing within one's own consciousness..."
If it is comprised within the category of afflictions (*kleśapakṣa*), it is called "coarseness" (*dausthulya*) and is also termed "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*).
If it belongs to the category of maturation (*vipākaja*), [it is not so termed].
Furthermore, those seeds comprised within other categories of the indeterminate (avyākṛta) are called only "gross heaviness" (dausthulya) and not "latent dispositions" (anuśaya).
This also applies to seeds comprised within wholesome factors such as faith (śraddhā) and so forth.
It is not termed "coarseness" (*dausthulya*), nor is it a "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*).
This is because when this dharma arises, the basis—
the personal continuum— is characterized solely by functional capacity and not by incapacity.

That treatise addresses only the non-grasping mind in terms of liberation from bondage;

Because these two arise by serving as mutual conditions for one another:
that is to say, with the characteristics (*nimitta*) as condition, the heavy burdens (*dausthulya*) arise;
and with the heavy burdens as condition, the bondage of characteristics arises.
The "bondage of signs" (*nimitta-bandhana*) refers to the manifest activity (*samudācāra*),

while the "heavy impediments" (dauṣṭhulya) are taken as the seeds (bīja).

The seeds of the two obstacles would not be eliminated.

It was previously stated that the bondage of signs consists of the grasping at the two natures.
One should carefully examine the contradictions among those various texts.
Here, "bondage by signs" refers to all contaminated signs (*sāsrava-nimitta*).
The "bond of coarseness" (dauṣṭhulya-bandhana) refers to the nature of all contaminated (sāsrava) states being fundamentally unstable;
it is identical to the "contaminated coarseness" described in the fifty-eighth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

One does not merely practice the differentiated contemplation of the four truths;
the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* speaks of both the conditioned and unconditioned four truths.
The unconditioned Four Noble Truths are non-positively established (*apratiṣṭhita*).
That which possesses distinctions and verbal designations is called "positively established" (*pratiṣṭhita*);
that which is without distinction and free from verbal designations is "non-positively established."
"Establishment" (vyavasthāna) means the sense of designation.
If a bodhisattva in this stage does not perform the two kinds of contemplation during their preparatory application (prayoga), [they do not establish it].
Because it cannot induce the arising of both the true and the phenomenal aspects,
nor can it subdue those of the two vehicles;
it is for the purpose of entering the contemplation of the two emptinesses and the principle of *tathatā*.

One correctly contemplates the non-established [dharmas] to give rise to the path of observation and the path of superior progress, thereby maturing the Buddha-dharmas and subduing those of the two vehicles; yet one also contemplates the established [dharmas].
However, as for those of the two vehicles, this is their own school’s position.
It is taught that [the śrāvaka] performs only the analytical meditation on the four truths as established entities;
the bodhisattva is not like this.
It is now taught that he also performs the non-established meditation on the emptiness of persons regarding them.
However, this is not the same as for a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva practices both types of emptiness;
because [the practitioner in question] is inferior to that, it is not mentioned here.
Furthermore, those of the two vehicles also merely perform provisional establishment,
unlike bodhisattvas;
for the conduct and wisdom of bodhisattvas are profound and vast.
Since that is not the case,

Because the Bodhisattva arises from this and enters the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

throughout the sixty-nine [stages], this is explained according to the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

can one enter the clear observation (abhisamaya) of the Noble Truths.
It is not the formless attainments.
Within the formless attainments,
śamatha is predominant and vipaśyanā is inferior.

thus it is stated in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Xuan-yang da-sheng fa-men lun), Chapter 16.
What is the basis for clear realization (*abhisamaya*)?
The answer is: it relies solely on the dhyānas and not on the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
If there are those who maintain that one can enter clear realization in all six stages, including the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*) and so forth—
Where in the text is there mention of being able to enter [the path] in the interim?
If one can enter clear realization (abhisamaya) within the six stages,
why does it say "only dhyāna" among the sixty-nine [categories]?
Furthermore, regarding the initial stage of the "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*),
how is it that among the seven types of realization (*abhisamaya*),
these six [realizations] are said to rely on the "not-yet-arrived" and the others? To what extent do they rely upon them?
Up to and including the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), a basis can be obtained.
Answer: One basis is obtainable as a non-basis;
all other bases are obtainable as bases.

and one type and one part are likewise. If,
in the intermediate dhyāna, there is reliance on a basis for entering the clear realization (abhisamaya).
It should be said that [the path] arises based on three or six foundations.

The sixth dhyāna is not mentioned to clarify that there is no entry into the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) within the intermediate dhyāna. Question: For what reason does one not enter [the path] by relying on the intermediate dhyāna? Answer: Because it lacks sharp, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
This is because those possessing sharp and clear untainted faculties are able to enter it;
furthermore, that Brahmā’s realm abounds in distraction and is not a ground of pure serenity.
The text of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that [the practitioner] relies upon the various dhyānas and the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*),
but does not mention the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*) because one enters the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) from there.
Regarding this, it is further stated that while the preliminary stage (*pūrvaprayoga*) pertains to all dhyānas,
it is only by relying on the fourth that it reaches fulfillment; thus,
at the time of final entry, one relies solely upon the fourth.
The fourth dhyāna is the most excellent among the remaining dhyānas, because one must rely upon this most excellent basis to enter the path of seeing;
thus, one does not enter it by relying on a lower stage. Therein lies the merit of the bodhisattva.
Sixty-nine [types of supernormal powers] are taught.
Although all dhyānas are capable of inducing them,
they are mostly based upon the fourth dhyāna.
This differs from the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
In the desire realm (kāmadhātu), there is no cultivation of wisdom, nor are there the four roots of goodness (kuśalamūla);
because they are untainted (anāsrava), it is not said that they depend on the bases (āyatana). This was previously stated among the twenty-two faculties (indriya).
The faculty of "knowing what is not yet known" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) extends to the formless realm,
because a bodhisattva attains it through cultivation alongside the path of seeing;
for if there were no path of seeing there, [it would not exist].
And regarding the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*):
for what reason is it said that one cultivates them?
It is stated in [the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*] 69:

When entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the seeds of all previously cultivated conventional wisdoms (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) become purified through that cultivation; this is also termed "cultivation.
This is called the conventional wisdom associated with the limit of the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).
Having emerged from the path of seeing, this wisdom arises;
from that point of generating the thought of enlightenment onwards,
it is all termed the faculty of "the unknown yet to be known" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
Because one sees the path while cultivating the previously acquired conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), this faculty is so named;
it indicates that when it was previously aroused, it was also called this faculty.
That is to say, conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) was already designated as this faculty prior to that time;
it is named this faculty when one enters the path of seeing (darśanamārga) and practices it concurrently.
This does not mean that there is a path of seeing in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
And [it includes] the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*).
Since the four roots of goodness are exclusively bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), this is based on one interpretation.
If that were so, then the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvyājñendriya*) should arise during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Now, upon reaching the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), they universally take all things as objects and are subsumed under the name "knowledge of what is already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). Furthermore, [the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*] states at sixty-nine:
When the first cognition of the path of seeing arises,
all other cognitions are said to be "transformed" because they are embraced by the conditions capable of producing it;
at this time, however, none of them are individually acquired.
Therefore, at the time of this path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are termed "cultivated" (*bhāvita*).
These are subsumed under these faculties. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter ten, states:
"The statement that those above are not cultivated is made from the perspective of the two vehicles (*yāna-dvaya*), which lack mastery."
If it is because the sovereign [knowledge] is first attained,
then cultivation also extends to the formless realms,
just as in the case of the object of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
As stated in the sixty-ninth [section],
this is the eighth ground of reliance.

Bodhisattvas rely exclusively on the fourth [dhyāna],
whereas the various treatises generally discuss it in terms of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).

whereas the others pertain to all [four] meditative concentrations and all stages (*bhūmi*). Thus says the treatise.

Commentary states:

Treatise:
Having attained mastery over many hundreds of gateways.
Commentary states:
Forty-seventh:
In a single instant, one realizes one hundred samādhis;
with the purified divine eye, one beholds the buddha-fields and sees one hundred Tathāgatas.
He can shake a hundred worlds and travel to those Buddha-fields,
emitting great rays of light and manifesting himself in a hundred forms so that all may see him,
thereby bringing a hundred kinds of sentient beings to spiritual maturity.
If one wishes to prolong one's life, one may abide for a hundred kalpas;
one perceives events throughout a hundred kalpas of the past and future limits;
and through wisdom and vision, one is able to enter the gate of illumination of a hundred dharmas.
He manifests a hundred bodies,
and each body can manifest a retinue of a hundred bodhisattvas;
he thus attains mastery over a thousand [powers].
The treatise is titled *The Many Hundred Gates*. It states:
"Know for yourself that before long you shall attain the benefit and happiness of all beings."
The commentary states:
Having realized suchness,
one immediately knows for oneself that one has realized it.
This is the practice for one's own benefit.
As it is taught in the sixty-ninth [sūtra] and others, even those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry can know this for themselves;
how much more so this bodhisattva?
Benefiting and bringing happiness to all is the practice of altruism.
A detailed explanation of its characteristics is as stated in the third [chapter] of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Therein, there are twelve hundred [verses].
That empowerment is of three kinds.
First is the empowerment of knowing the spiritual power of a hundred Buddhas;
herein, one directly perceives the gathering of a hundred Buddhas.
Second, he adds the ability to enter a hundred Buddha-worlds,
which is included within the aforementioned shaking of a hundred worlds.
Third, he adds the illumination of a hundred Buddha-worlds.
It is also included within the movement of a hundred worlds.
Furthermore, that [previous stage] matures fewer than this [current stage] in terms of the hundred types of sentient beings to be converted.
